common_name: Cucuzza (Italian Edible Gourd, Sicilian Snake Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, giving the sprawling vine a sturdy arbor or fence so the long, pale-green fruit can hang straight rather than curl on the ground.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, and give the sprawling vine a sturdy arbor or fence so the long, pale-green fruit can hang straight rather than curl on the ground. Cucuzza is a long-season Italian-American heirloom bottle gourd grown throughout Louisiana's historically Sicilian communities, where the immature fruit is peeled and cooked like a mild summer squash in soups, stews, and sautés. Left on the vine past the edible stage, the mature shell dries into a hard, lightweight gourd useful for crafts. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and, like other bottle gourds, benefits from hand-pollination in the evening since its flowers open at night for moth pollinators.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Marion Tomato (NC State Southern-Adapted Disease-Resistant Tomato)

planting.note: Start seed indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50°F, staking or caging the compact determinate plants as fruit sets.

directions: Start seed indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50°F, staking or caging the compact determinate plants as fruit sets. Marion was bred at North Carolina State University and released for Southern gardens, combining Fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot resistance with reliable fruit set under the hot, humid conditions that cause many slicing tomatoes to falter. The medium-sized, deep-red fruit has firm flesh and balanced flavor well suited to fresh eating and canning. Because it sets a concentrated main crop, it remains a dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want an early, disease-resistant harvest before peak summer heat shuts down fruit set.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: African Runner Peanut (Historic Small-Seeded Heirloom Peanut)

planting.note: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods.

directions: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods. This small-seeded heirloom peanut traces to peanuts brought to the American South through the transatlantic slave trade and was documented growing at Monticello in Jefferson's own garden notes, making it one of the oldest peanut lines still in American cultivation. Its bushy, low-spreading habit and heavy yield of small, sweet, easy-shelling pods make it well suited to home-scale roasting and boiling, and the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season matches its full maturity window better than most northern gardens can offer.
sources: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello Center for Historic Plants

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season.

directions: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season. This dark-green, deeply ribbed Japanese heirloom shares Cucurbita moschata's excellent resistance to vine borers and squash bugs with better-known Gulf-adapted moschata types, making it a strong performer where humidity and pests knock out C. maxima and C. pepo squash. The dense, sweet orange flesh stores for months after curing in a warm, dry spot. Its heat tolerance and disease resistance make it a good companion or alternative to Seminole pumpkin for zone 8-10 gardeners wanting variety in their moschata winter squash.

common_name: Hanover Salad Green (Colonial-Era Southern Heirloom Salad Green)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves.

directions: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves. Hanover Salad is a colonial-era Southern heirloom green in the same species as rutabaga, prized historically in Virginia and Gulf South gardens for its mild, cabbage-like flavor eaten raw as salad greens when young or cooked like collards once mature. It tolerates both cold snaps and the on-and-off warmth of a Gulf Coast fall and winter better than many mustards, holding quality in the garden for extended picking rather than bolting at the first warm spell.

common_name: Shunkyo Semi-Long Radish (Japanese Rose-Pink Heirloom Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding.

directions: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding. This Japanese heirloom produces rose-pink, tapered roots four to five inches long with crisp, notably sweet and mild flesh that holds its quality and stays crisp longer than typical round spring radishes as temperatures fluctuate. Its extended harvest window and resistance to turning pithy or overly hot in warm soil make it a reliable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners working with a short, mild winter rather than a true hard freeze. Both the roots and the peppery young leaves are edible.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
